newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish Peasant party rejects 1998 budget proposals.
newsitem.headline: Polish Peasant party rejects 1998 budget proposals.

text.p: The Polish Peasant Party (PSL), junior partner in the ruling coalition, on Wednesday rejected government proposals for the 1998 budget and told its ministers to vote against them in cabinet, its spokesman said.

PAP news agency quoted spokesman Aleksander Bentkowski as saying the PSL executive committee had adopted a resolution criticising assumptions about the economy put to the cabinet by the finance ministry as it prepares a budget draft.
"The PSL cannot support these assumptions," he said.

The Peasants' four-year-long governing coalition with the larger Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) of former communists has shown mounting strains and is uncertain to survive general elections on September 21.
The party's executive committee said moves envisaged in the preliminary budget proposals to cap domestic demand could slow economic growth and harm the financial situation of firms.
Finance Minister Marek Belka said on Wednesday the proposals included a cut in the budget deficit to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1998 from 2.8 percent planned for the current year.
The aim is to dampen internal demand to curb a recent steep rise in the current account deficit, which Belka expects to reach $6 billion and the end of 1997 compared with $1.35 billion in 1996.
The Peasants' leader Waldemar Pawlak also said the proposals, full details of which have not yet been made public, could increase unemployment and would not stimulate exports, PAP reported.

The party said the finance ministry was suggesting that the independent central bank should maintain high real official interest rates against a background of falling inflation, arguing that this would hamper investment.
It objected to the ministry's proposals on agriculture, charging that they would hinder rural restructuring, the development of technical infrastructure and hence rural job creation, PAP reported.
Belka told a news briefing he was confident the cabinet at its session on Thursday would approve the budget's macroeconomic assumptions and proposed revenue and spending.
He hopes the government will be able to submit the full budget with plans for individual ministries to parliament by the end of September.
Although the Peasants and the SLD are both rooted in the pre-1989 communist system, they have grown apart ideologically.

The Peasants, keen to stay in power to champion interests of their rural or small-town supporters, could form a new coalition with the powerful right-leaning opposition grouped around the Solidarity trade union -- Solidarity Election Action (AWS).
